title: Role of sodium-calcium exchanger for impulse conduction in the sinoatrial node of adult mice Impulse conduction in the sinoatrial node
content:
by Georgina Haviar, Martina Maass, Gabriel Peinkofer, Marcel Halbach, Claudia Schubert-Quecke, Joshua I. Goldhaber, Kenneth D. Philipson, Hannes Reuter, Sabine Groenke

The sodium-calcium exchanger is the primary mechanism for removing calcium from the cell. Its role in impulse generation (ignition/pacing) of the sinoatrial node has been actively discussed, but the significance for impulse conduction is unknown. A deeper understanding of these mechanisms is essential for understanding the pathophysiology underlying the resulting sinus node dysfunction. In the long term, this could lay the groundwork for pharmacological treatment of these conditions, which to date mostly require the implantation of a pacemaker. To investigate impulse conduction we perform immunofluorescence and fibrotic histological stainings and correlate our findings with electrophysiological data of sharp electrode measurements in the intact sinoatrial node from atrial-specific sodium–calcium exchanger knockout mice. Successful impulse conduction requires overcoming the source/sink mismatch between sinoatrial node and atrial myocardium. Sinoatrial node from knockout shows a significantly higher degree of fibrosis as well as an altered connexin distribution (trend towards a decrease of Connexin 40 in the right atrium, trend towards an increase of Connexin 45 and significant increase of Connexin 40 in the HCN4 positive sinoatrial node), which might have an impact on impaired impulse conduction. Sharp electrode measurements reveal that there are no pacemaker potentials in the sinus node of adult sodium–calcium exchanger knockout mice (sinus arrest) but spontaneous action potentials at the borders to the atria with a typical burst-pause pattern. An atrial-specific knockout of sodium–calcium exchanger appears to influence the source-sink relationship, which can lead to impaired sinoatrial conduction and thus to sinus node dysfunction. Various factors seem to play a role here: altered connexin expression, fibrosis and impaired coupling of membrane and calcium clock possibly due to altered calcium homeostasis. Therefore we conclude that the sodium–calcium exchanger is important not only for the impulse generation, but also for its conduction.
